title: Upgradeability and who controls the upgrade
reason: Grep for `update_current_contract_wasm|deploy_v2|contractmeta` across src/ returns zero hits outside comments. rust.ts collects only #[contract]/#[contractimpl]/#[contracttype]/#[contracterror]/#[contractevent]/contractimport! (analyseRustFile, lines 72-117); nothing detects a deployer() call. ContractData (types.ts:114-121) is {crate, wasmPath, localWasmHash, functions} — no upgradeable/upgradeFn/meta. Partial coverage exists and should temper the fix: a `pub fn upgrade(...)` already becomes a function node with params/returns/requiresAuth and is printed by contextDigest (query.ts:378-383) and list_contracts, and signals()'s mutating regex (query.ts:273) already includes `upgrade`, so an unauthed one is flagged; fetchMeta (cli.ts:118-129) + flattenMeta already captures arbitrary contractmeta key/vals including `binver`, but only for a *deployed* contract when online with an alias, stored on DeploymentData.meta and rendered at render.ts:209-212. What is genuinely absent: whether the contract is upgradeable at all when the entry point is named `migrate`/`set_wasm` rather than `upgrade`, and the factory relationship — `deploy_v2` produces a structural contract-deploys-contract edge that architecture() cannot see. Both are literal, high-confidence tokens, read-only, Soroban-specific.
pattern: `env.deployer().update_current_contract_wasm(new_wasm_hash)`, `contractmeta!(key = "binver", val = ...)`, `env.deployer().with_address(..).deploy_v2(..)` (factory), SEP-0049 upgrade interface
why_it_matters: Whether a contract is mutable is the first fact that gates every other decision, and it is invisible in the current graph — `deployer()` appears nowhere in the scanner. If the contract IS upgradeable, live state written by the old code exists, so an agent that reshapes a `#[contracttype]` breaks decoding on chain; if it is NOT upgradeable, a bug found today can never be patched and the whole conversation changes. The memory should record: upgradeable yes/no, which function performs the upgrade, which address it auths, whether a schema/version key is stored, and the source `contractmeta!` values — which can be cross-checked against `stellar contract info meta` (already fetched into `DeploymentData.meta` but never compared with source).

title: Which address require_auth actually authorizes (not a boolean)
reason: rust.ts:349 is the whole implementation: `requiresAuth: /\brequire_auth(_for_args)?\s*\(/.test(fnBody)`. The receiver expression is never captured, and require_auth_for_args is collapsed into the same boolean. FunctionData (types.ts:133-140) carries only `requiresAuth: boolean`; render.ts:167-170 prints 'Calls require_auth, so this entry point is access-controlled' — which is exactly the false reassurance the security doc warns about, since `who.require_auth()` on a caller-supplied `who` proves nothing about privilege. Existing coverage is the inverse case only: signals() (query.ts:271-281) flags mutating functions with *no* auth at all, so `deposit(user, amount)` with zero require_auth is caught; `deposit` that authenticates the wrong subject is invisible. The fix is cheap and reliable: the receiver token is textually adjacent to `.require_auth()`, params are already parsed by parseParams, and collectLetBindings (rust.ts:449-461) already exists to resolve `let admin = storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Admin)` — the same machinery canonicaliseKey uses.
pattern: `admin.require_auth()` where `admin` is a storage-loaded value vs. a caller-supplied `Address` parameter; `require_auth_for_args`; `authorize_as_current_contract`
why_it_matters: `FunctionData.requiresAuth` is a single boolean from `/\brequire_auth(_for_args)?\s*\(/` — it records THAT auth happened, never WHOSE. That makes the memory confidently wrong on the skill's headline anti-pattern. In the shipped demo, `Treasury::initialize(env, admin: Address)` calls `admin.require_auth()` on its own parameter; the memory reports "requires auth" and `signals()` says nothing, yet anyone can call it and become admin. The scanner already has `collectLetBindings()`, so it can classify the auth subject as (a) a fn parameter, (b) a value read from a storage key, or (c) `current_contract_address()` — a hard, checkable fact. The same pass should record which `Address` params are forwarded into a cross-contract client call without being auth'd locally, which is the skill's most-common-real-bug.

reason: Confirmed absent. collectAttributed (rust.ts:247-258) matches only the attribute plus `enum <Name>` and returns NamedDecl {name, line} — the body is never read, so no variants and no `= N` codes. scan.ts:331-341 creates the error node with a fixed summary and no `data` field at all. Partial coverage keeps this at medium rather than high: the error node carries path+line so describe_node hands the developer the exact file:line to open, and function `returns` already shows `Result<(), Error>` in contextDigest and list_contracts. The 'never renumber across upgrades' hazard is real but bites at upgrade time, not at context-recovery time, and the enum is one file open away.
pattern: `#[contracterror] #[repr(u32)] enum E { NotInitialized = 1, ... }`; on-chain `udt_error_enum_v0` cases
why_it_matters: The memory stores only the enum's name (`error:PayrollError`) — not a single variant, not a single discriminant. Yet those integers are a published ABI that callers match on, and the skill's rule is absolute. There is also no link from functions to the errors they can return: `EdgeKind` declares `raises` but `scan.ts` never emits it, so "what can this call fail with" is unanswerable. Storing the variant→code map from source and diffing it against the deployed spec makes "someone renumbered an error code" a hard, detectable fact rather than an audit finding.

title: Event shape: topics vs data payload, not just the event name
reason: Confirmed on both paths. Source side: #[contractevent] goes through collectAttributed, so struct fields and #[topic] markers are never read (the `(?:\([^)]*\))?` in the regex tolerates `#[contractevent(topics = [..])]` but discards the args); parseEvents (rust.ts:483-495) takes splitTopLevel(args,',')[0] and reduces it via eventName() to a single symbol literal, throwing away the remaining topics and the entire data argument. On-chain side the claim is precisely right and the fix is nearly free: spec.ts already models the full shape — SpecEvent.prefix_topics, SpecEvent.data_format, and SpecParam.location: 'topic_list' | 'data' (spec.ts:20,32-39) — and scan.ts:869 collapses it to `events: spec.events.map((e) => e.name)`. So the tool parses the layout and then deletes it. Value is medium not high: a wrong event shape breaks indexers and wallets silently, but it is a build-time correctness concern more than something a returning developer is blocked on, and the event node with its name and file:line already gets them to the declaration.
pattern: `#[contractevent]` with `#[topic]` field markers, `#[contractevent(topics = [..])]`, `data_format = "map"|"vec"|"single-value"`; the SEP-41 standard event shapes; the deprecated `env.events().publish(topics, data)` form
why_it_matters: `collectAttributed(src, 'contractevent')` records the struct name and nothing else, and `parseEvents` pulls only the first topic symbol out of the deprecated publish form. So the memory knows an event called `paid` exists but not which fields are topics, in what order, or how the data is encoded — which is precisely the contract that indexers and wallets are wired against and precisely what a refactor breaks silently. Here too the data is already parsed and thrown away: `spec.ts` reads `prefix_topics`, `params[].location: 'topic_list'|'data'` and `data_format`, and `scan.ts` reduces it to `spec.events.map(e => e.name)`. Recording the full shape also lets the memory note when a contract still uses the deprecated `events().publish` API (the demo does).

title: TTL extension arguments, bounded variants, and instance-storage misuse
reason: Real, and it is currently producing wrong output, not just missing output. I ran the parseStorage regex (rust.ts:422-423) against real inputs: (a) `extend_ttl_with_limits(&key, ...)` does NOT match, because the alternation requires `extend_ttl` followed immediately by optional turbofish then `(` — so a protocol-26 contract that correctly extends its TTL is recorded as having no extension, and signals() (query.ts:251-260) plus render.ts:183-187 then emit a false 'can expire and become unreachable' warning about correct code; (b) `env.storage().instance().extend_ttl(100, 5184000)` matches, and since instance TTL takes no key, firstArg captures the threshold — I confirmed it yields key '100', creating a junk storage node titled '100 (instance)' that flows into storage_layout and contextDigest. The threshold/extend_to values themselves are captured into `args` at rust.ts:430 and then dropped, and StorageData (types.ts:125-131) has only {durability, key, hasTtlExtension}. This matters more than the other items because the persistent-TTL warning is one of the tool's four flagship signals and is named in the project_signals MCP description (mcp.ts:194-196); it is currently both false-positive-prone and polluting the storage list.
pattern: `extend_ttl(threshold, extend_to)` numeric args in ledgers (17,280/day; ~180-day / 3,110,400 ceiling), `extend_ttl_with_limits` (protocol 26+), and parameterized keys stored in `instance()`
why_it_matters: `StorageData.hasTtlExtension` is a boolean, so the memory says "ttl extended" for the demo's `extend_ttl(&key, 100_000, 200_000)` — 5.8 days threshold, 11.6 days ceiling, far under the ~120-day convention — and a returning developer has no way to recall whether that was deliberate. The numbers are the forgettable part. Two correctness items ride along: (1) the storage regex enumerates `get|try_get|set|has|remove|update|extend_ttl` only, so a contract using `extend_ttl_with_limits` is reported as never extending its TTL — a false warning on the tool's own headline signal; (2) an `instance()` key that carries a parameter (`DataKey::Balance(Address)`) is per-entity data in a single 64KB ledger entry, which the skill rules out flatly, and the scanner already canonicalises key expressions so the argument is right there.

title: Standard-interface conformance of the project's own contracts (SEP-41 / SEP-40 / SEP-50 / SEP-56)
reason: Nothing compares a function set against an interface table. `ContractData` (types.ts:114-121) is only `{crate, wasmPath, localWasmHash, functions: string[]}`; stellar/spec.ts only shapes SCSpecEntry into `functions/events/structs/...` with no conformance logic; query.ts `signals()` (237-285) checks exactly four things — drift, persistent-without-extend_ttl, mutating-without-require_auth, contracts-with-no-tests. It is a pure set comparison over data already collected (scan.ts:219 stores the parsed fn names; `fetchInterface` already returns the compiled spec), so it is read-only and reliably detectable. Value is only medium, not high: `contextDigest` (query.ts:378-383) already prints every signature with params and return type, so a returning developer reading `transfer(from, to, amount)` / `balance(id)` already knows it is a token. The genuinely new fact is the *missing required function* delta (e.g. a SEP-41 token with no `burn_from`), which is the part that would break wallet/SAC interop.
pattern: Fingerprint each contract's exported function set against a table of standard interfaces and record which standard it conforms to, plus which required functions are missing. SEP-41 token = {allowance, approve, balance, transfer, transfer_from, burn, burn_from, decimals, name, symbol}; SEP-40 oracle = {lastprice, prices, decimals, assets, resolution}; SEP-56 vault = deposit/withdraw/redeem/total_assets shape. Prefer the compiled/on-chain spec from `stellar contract info interface` over the parsed `pub fn` list when available.
why_it_matters: A SEP-41 contract's function set is a public ABI: every wallet, SAC-interop path and DEX integration depends on the exact names. An agent asked to "rename `transfer_from` to something clearer" has no way to know it is standing on a standard, and a returning developer forgets that the token crate was deliberately shaped to SEP-41. Nothing in the model expresses conformance — ContractData carries only `crate`, `wasmPath`, `localWasmHash`, `functions`. It also makes a new high-value signal possible: "Token claims SEP-41 but exposes no `allowance`."

title: Dependence on protocol-gated or draft host functions (CAP-51 / 59 / 74 / 75)
reason: Genuinely absent: rust.ts inspects a function body with exactly three matchers — `parseStorage` (419), `parseEvents` (483), `parseClientCalls` (511) — plus the `require_auth` test at line 349. A grep for bls12/secp256r1/bn254/poseidon across src returns nothing. It is detectable with the same regex vocabulary already used for `storage().instance().get(` and is strictly read-only. pattern: Flag use of `soroban_sdk::crypto` host functions whose availability is protocol- and network-dependent: `crypto().bls12_381()` (CAP-59), `bn254` (CAP-74, proposal), Poseidon (CAP-75, proposal), secp256r1 signature verification (CAP-51, passkeys), together with the `soroban-sdk` version requirement cargo.ts already parses. A returning developer who left a passkey or ZK branch pinned to futurenet has no record of *why* mainnet was not the target, and an agent that regenerates or ports the code needs to know the primitive is gated before assuming it will deploy. The skill explicitly asks that this be written down rather than rediscovered. Nothing in rust.ts looks at `env.crypto()` at all, and the SDK version is stored on the crate node without any link to what the code actually requires from the host.

reason: Narrowly real. `contractmeta!` is never read: `collectAttributed` (rust.ts:78-80) handles only contracttype/contracterror/contractevent, and `collectImports` (289) matches only `contractimport!`, so no source-declared meta key reaches the graph. title: Token/SAC client calls are parsed, then silently discarded — the value path is invisible
reason: Confirmed by running dist/scanner/rust.js against a TokenClient/StellarAssetClient/token::Client fixture. parseClientCalls (src/scanner/rust.ts:511-522, regex /\b(\w+)\s*::\s*Client\s*::\s*new\s*\(|\b(\w+)Client\s*::\s*new\s*\(/g) DOES capture them — it yields clientCalls: ["Token"], ["StellarAsset"], ["token"]. But the name dies there: (a) clientCalls is never copied into FunctionData (src/core/types.ts:133-140 has only params/returns/requiresAuth/visibility), and (b) its sole consumer, linkCrossContractCalls at src/scanner/scan.ts:525-536, does `const target = resolve(client); if (!target || target === fromId) continue;` — resolve() only looks up local #[contract] nodes by normalised name/crate/wasm filename, so "Token"/"StellarAsset" never resolve and the edge is dropped with no node, no edge, no warning. Nothing in render.ts, query.ts contextDigest or mcp.ts ever sees a token client. So mcp.ts's list_contracts promise of 'cross-contract calls' silently omits the most common outbound call in Soroban. Partial mitigation only: the Address-typed params (asset_contract: Address) and storage keys like DataKey::PayToken do appear in contextDigest, so the value path is dimly inferable, not stated.
pattern: `soroban_sdk::token::Client` / `TokenClient::new(&env, &asset_contract)` and `token::StellarAssetClient::new(...)` — the SEP-41/SAC interface a contract uses to move value
why_it_matters: The single most important thing about a DeFi/payroll/treasury contract is which external token contract it moves money through, and that fact is currently thrown away. I confirmed by running the shipped parser: `TokenClient::new`, `StellarAssetClient::new`, and `token::Client::new` produce clientCalls of `"Token"`, `"StellarAsset"`, `"token"`, none of which resolve to a workspace contract in `linkCrossContractCalls`, so no edge is created and no node exists. title: No standard-conformance fact (SEP-41 / SEP-50) — and a trait-based token contract currently records zero functions
reason: The second half is a confirmed parser defect, verified by execution. Fed `#[contract] pub struct MyToken;` plus `#[contractimpl] impl token::TokenInterface for MyToken { fn balance(...) fn transfer(...) fn decimals(...) }`, analyseRustFile returns contracts: [{ name: 'MyToken', line: 4, functions: [] }]. Two causes: parseImplFunctions (src/scanner/rust.ts:324) matches `/\bpub\s+fn\s+(\w+)\s*(?:<[^>]*>)?\s*\(/g`, but Rust forbids visibility modifiers on trait-impl methods, so no trait method can ever match; and collectContractImpls (src/scanner/rust.ts:269) captures the token after `impl` — for `impl token::TokenInterface for MyToken` that is the TRAIT (typeName 'TokenInterface'), not the implementing type, so even if functions were found they would be filed under a phantom contract that the filter at rust.ts:112-114 then discards. Downstream this renders as render.ts:142 '_No public functions detected._' on a token contract — actively misleading, not merely incomplete. The conformance-labelling half (a new src/stellar/standards.ts, ContractData.conformsTo) is a derived nicety on top and is worth far less than the parse fix.
pattern: Matching a contract's exported function set against the SEP-41 token interface the skill enumerates; `#[contractimpl] impl token::TokenInterface for MyToken`
why_it_matters: Memory should say 'Contract X conforms to SEP-41 (7/7)' or 'implements 6 of 7, missing `approve`' — that is what tells a returning developer whether wallets/DEXes/anchors can use their token, and what stops an agent from renaming a function and silently breaking ecosystem compatibility. Worse, the idiomatic way to write such a contract is invisible today: I ran the shipped parser on `#[contractimpl] impl token::TokenInterface for MyToken { fn balance(..) .. }` and got `{ name: "MyToken", functions: [] }`. Two compounding causes — `collectContractImpls`'s `impl(?:\s*<[^>]*>)?\s+([\w:]+)` binds the *trait* path (`TokenInterface`) rather than the implementing type, and `parseImplFunctions` requires `\bpub\s+fn`, which trait-impl methods never carry. Result: a token contract shows an empty public interface, and the `require_auth` signal never fires on `transfer` or `approve`. Ground truth is already available for cross-checking — `spec.ts` parses typed `function_v0` entries but they are only stashed on the deployment node.
where_to_implement: src/scanner/rust.ts (`collectContractImpls` + `parseImplFunctions`); new src/stellar/standards.ts holding the SEP-41/SEP-50 signatures; src/scanner/scan.ts and src/stellar/spec.ts consumers; src/core/types.ts (`ContractData.conformsTo`); src/core/query.ts and src/commands/mcp.ts

title: Event schemas are reduced to a bare name — the topic tuple and data payload are thrown away twice
reason: Both discard points verified. Source side: parseEvents (rust.ts:483-495) keeps only `splitTopLevel(args, ',')[0]` — the topic tuple — and then eventName (rust.ts:503-509) collapses it to the `Symbol::new`/`symbol_short!` literal, so in `publish((Symbol::new(&env,"paid"), employee), amount)` both the `employee` topic and the `amount` data argument are dropped; scan.ts:299-316 stores the resulting string with no `data` payload at all (demo index.json shows `event:Payroll.paid` with `data: undefined`). Partial coverage exists only in the fallback branch, where a tuple with no symbol literal survives as raw text. Spec side: spec.ts:32-39 fully parses `prefix_topics`, `params[].location: 'topic_list'|'data'` and `data_format`, and scan.ts:867-870 throws all of it away with `events: spec.events.map((e) => e.name)`. Topic arity and order are what a getEvents filter is built from and cannot be recalled without reopening the contract.
pattern: A Soroban event is a positional topic tuple plus a data value. `env.events().publish((Symbol::new(&env,"paid"), employee), amount)` is topics `["paid", Address]` and data `i128`. The compiled spec expresses the same thing as `event_v0 { prefix_topics, params[].location: 'topic_list' | 'data', data_format }`.
why_it_matters: src/scanner/rust.ts:483-509 takes only the first argument of `publish(...)` and collapses it to the first symbol literal, so `employee` (a topic) and `amount` (the data) are lost. Worse, the ground-truth path already parses `prefix_topics`, `params[].location` and `data_format` in spec.ts:32-39 and then discards them: recordDeployment (scan.ts:869) stores only `events: spec.events.map(e => e.name)`. Anyone writing or maintaining a getEvents filter needs the topic arity and positions — the filter is matched segment by segment, so adding a topic silently breaks every consumer. This is the schema a developer cannot reconstruct from memory after two weeks, and the fix is mostly deleting a `.map(e => e.name)`.
where_to_implement: src/scanner/rust.ts `parseEvents` (return the full topic tuple elements and the data argument, not just `eventName`); src/core/types.ts (an `EventData { topics: string[]; dataType?: string; declaredVia: 'publish' | 'contractevent' }`); src/scanner/scan.ts:299-316 (store it) and scan.ts:862-875 (keep `spec.events` in full, and flag source-vs-spec disagreement the way wasm-hash drift is flagged); expose via a new MCP tool or in `describe_node`.
